name: Emergency card, sitter sheet and school-form kit from one set of family pages
description: From one set of family pages in the shared handbook, Happy helps a parent produce the pages other people ask for: a one-page emergency plan to print, a sheet to hand to a sitter or other carer, and, for school forms, a list of where each document is and when it runs out, a checklist of open forms and the answers as one block to paste. The parent prints, forwards, signs and submits. Happy is never the emergency channel: it is told to start its reply to a text that sounds like an emergency with a line to call emergency services or Poison Help.
example: A parent texts 'make the sitter sheet for Friday' and gets one message to forward or print. Jordan texts: 'What do I still need for the third-grader's school forms?' and gets the open items from that child's page. A parent who texts 'He swallowed something, what do I do?' gets a reply that starts with the line to call emergency services or Poison Help, and then the answer.
how: Facts: a plan page and a page per child in the shared handbook (F043), read-only for the agents: contacts, the doctor's office, each official document's place and valid-until date, and the open forms. No allergies, medicines or conditions: a parent writes those onto a sheet by hand. Emergency plan: an interview following Ready.gov's four steps ends with the finished page in one message; the parent prints or saves it, and Tony pastes it into the folder, without health lines, if Happy should reuse it. Sitter sheet: an AGENTS.md prompt template over the same pages. Form kit: a form sent as a photo or PDF (F002) gets its answers drafted as one block to paste, drafts only; a due date is an ordinary reminder (F007, Tony only). Emergency texts: one AGENTS.md line (start the reply with 'call emergency services or Poison Help', then answer) and one more eval case, vaguely worded. No hook, phrase list, database row or house-rules rule.
depends_on: F043 shared family handbook (the plan page and the two children's pages live there, typed or pasted in by Tony)
Tony provides the facts for those pages at execution: emergency contacts, the doctor's office, where each official document is kept and its valid-until date
Tony provides a check of the poison-help number at execution, before the sheet is printed
F002 photo and PDF reading, for a form sent as a photo or PDF

Optional: F009 calendar read for 'tonight's plan' on the sitter sheet; F007 reminders for a form's due date and a yearly contact re-check (Tony only, since Jordan is not a command owner); F080 printing, and until it exists a parent prints the page from a phone
caveats: Happy can be down in exactly the events that matter, since a power cut stops the Mac and a network outage stops iMessage, so the printed sheet is the part that survives, and the phone's own emergency call and medical ID features remain the right tools.

There is no canned emergency reply: the 'call emergency services' line comes from the cloud model under one instruction with eval cases, so it is not a limit, and there is no reply at all while the model is down.
The poison-help number on the printed sheet comes from the poison centre's own page listed in the sources, and a parent checks it before the sheet is printed.
Only Tony adds or changes a stored page: a parent saves or prints the finished page and tells Tony when a fact changes. Happy cannot update a page itself.

Children's health details are not stored, the default Tony left in place (he lifted it for the dose log only), so a parent writes allergies, medicines and conditions onto the printed sheet by hand. Whatever a parent types into the chat to finish a sheet or an answer block still reaches the cloud model, and so does a form sent as a photo or PDF; the house rule on the printed sheet asks parents not to send medical papers.

Happy never signs, fills in or submits a form; the drafts-only rule is a prompt instruction that holds only because the agent has no tool that could fill in or send one. Requirements differ by state, district and organiser, so Happy lists what each form asked for last time and does not know the rules. ID, policy and certificate numbers and the Wi-Fi password stay off these pages.
safety: The pages hold contacts and document details, no children's health facts; they stay in the handbook folder, read only by the parents' own agents, and on paper. Drafting from them sends those facts to the cloud model; an instruction keeps them from the research helper. Happy messages nobody outside the family: a parent forwards the sheet and submits every form. No tool is added.
unverified: That a parent's sandboxed agent can search and read pages in the shared handbook folder (F043's own first test, part of T6); these pages rest on it.
That the new eval case with vague wording ('he swallowed something') gets the emergency line first; the existing swallowed-battery case already passes with no instruction.
The federal Poison Help site refused automated fetches, so the poison-help number comes from the National Capital Poison Center's page listed in the sources and has to be checked by a parent.
What the school's own forms ask for, and whether the state's immunization registry gives parents direct online access; seen with the first real form.

name: Operator self-checks: a daily Google sign-in check, with audits and drills run by Tony
description: One daily check on the Mac tells Tony, and only Tony, when a Google sign-in that Happy's mail or calendar reading depends on has stopped working, so an expired sign-in does not first show up as a missing or empty morning text. The security audit (after every update and each month), the monthly checklist and the quarterly restore drill and key rotation stay commands Tony runs himself, prompted by reminders on his own calendar. Behaviour test cases join the existing eval suite when the feature they test ships, and are run on demand and after a critical-path change, as already decided.
example: Trigger: the stored Google sign-in for one parent's Gmail stops working. Within a day the check raises an alert on Tony's phone through ntfy, the route his other alerts use, and nothing is sent to the family. That parent approves the sign-in again on Google's screen and the next run is clean.
how: A daily launchd job runs one read-only script as the happy user, as the sandbox check and the eval job in the config repo already do. It runs `gog auth list --check` and reads every entry (its exit status does not prove every sign-in valid), then reports as those checks do: one ok-or-not metric for a Grafana rule, or a counts-only line to ntfy. It covers each sign-in as it is added: Tony's mail, Jordan's mail, then the calendar sign-ins. No scheduler job, no model call, no text from Happy, no house-rules rule. Go-live test: a sign-in broken on purpose raises the alert within a day and nothing reaches the family. Not jobs: the security audit (after every update and monthly), the monthly checklist (spend caps, new stores in the backup, standing approvals) and the quarterly restore drill and key rotation; Tony runs these from calendar reminders. Behaviour cases: each feature adds its own eval case when it ships; none is built ahead.
caveats: The five-minute dead-man probe and the M1 Grafana alerts already cover 'gateway down' and 'iMessage unhealthy'. The only new signal here is the Google sign-in; do not build the same alert twice.
The check cannot run until gog is installed and a sign-in is stored; gog is not on the Mac mini today.

Given up with this form: a daily look at the model sign-in, the channel probe and plugin load state (Tony looks at plugin load state after each deploy instead), automatic comparison of audit results between runs, and results arriving in the iMessage thread.

The monthly and quarterly items are reminder lines, not a feature: spend caps, the daily budget alert and the nightly verified backup already exist. The backup archive holds sign-ins and keys unencrypted and must never be copied to iCloud.
Plain doctor can migrate state, so the by-hand checks use its lint form, as happy-inspect already does.

Behaviour cases run the real model and cost tokens on every run, and the daily cost alert does not see eval-clone spend; eval clones must keep messaging tools denied, or a reminder test would text the family.
unverified: gog is not installed on the Mac mini today; `gog auth list --check` and what it prints for each entry are known from the bundled gog skill, and must be confirmed on the installed version.

Whether that check notices a sign-in that Google has revoked or only reads what is stored on the Mac; the go-live test (a sign-in broken on purpose must raise the alert within a day and send nothing to the family) settles it.

How a launchd job run as the happy user reads the stored sign-ins: the bundled gog skill says a run without a desktop keyring needs gog's file keyring and its password in the environment; not tried on this Mac.
If the calendar sign-in is stored apart from the mail one (as the calendar card plans), whether one run of the check lists both or the script has to look in two places.
How promptfoo's tool-trajectory assertions behave against 2026.9.7 (an open item in the roadmap), for the behaviour cases added later.
safety: The check is read-only and runs on the host: no agent gains exec or any other tool, no model reads its output, and the result goes only to Tony, as a count or an ok-or-not signal with no mail content. Behaviour cases added later call the model only against eval clones with fake users and fake secrets.

name: Weekly 'what Happy did' text
description: Once a week Tony gets one short text that counts what Happy's tools did for him that week and lists the saved-note files that changed, written by a small script with no model. There is no journal and no 'undo that', and forgetting a conversation stays Tony's command at the Mac. Jordan's copy is a second job of the same kind, about her own agent only, added when she asks.
example: The weekly text, starting with its own label: 'What Happy did this week: web search 9 calls, research helper 3, weather 12, scheduling tool 4. Notes changed: 2 files', followed by the two file names. In a week with nothing to count, no text is sent.
how: One checked-in script, no model and no agent tool. It asks OpenClaw's own activity record for the past week of that parent's agent (`openclaw audit --agent <id> --kind tool_action --status succeeded --after <date> --json`, paging with `--limit` and `--cursor`), counts finished calls by tool name, and lists by name the files changed that week in that parent's notes folder (F041). The jobs script (G003) creates one command job for Tony: his handle read from the family file, a time limit, the day and daytime hour he names, the text starting with its own label, and `NO_REPLY` when there is nothing to count. Jordan's copy is a second job from the same script, about her own agent, added when she asks. The query is tried once from a scheduled command job before the script is written. Not built: a journal table, a copy of note text, an undo tool, a read tool on any agent. House-rules plugin: no rule needed.
caveats: Counts are by tool name only: the text says 'scheduling tool 4 calls', not which reminder or list, and a built-in tool that does several things under one name is one line. In-house tools should give each kind of write its own tool name so the counts mean something.
A note file changed twice in one week counts once, and the text shows file names, not what was saved.
There is no 'undo that'. A parent says 'cancel that reminder' or 'change it back to X' and the tool that made the change does it; an item Happy added to a list can be deleted on the phone.
Nothing answers 'what did you do this week?' exactly in mid-week: no agent gets a tool that reads the record. 'What did you save about me?' is answered from that parent's own notes (F041).
The activity record is on by default, holds no content and keeps 30 days, so the text cannot look further back than that.
Forgetting works per conversation and stays Tony's command at the Mac (`openclaw memory forget`, with `--dry-run` first); nothing is built for it here.
corrections: 'Forget what I said about X works' (9 Oct description) is not a platform ability: memory forget selects whole sessions by id, hook source or participant, never by topic or message text, and reworded copies are outside its cleanup. Topic-level forgetting is a hand edit of the memory file.

'Promote via openclaw memory promote --apply' will usually promote nothing a parent just confirmed: by default a candidate needs a 0.75 score, three recalls and three distinct queries. Either pass lower thresholds or write the confirmed line to MEMORY.md directly.
unverified: That `openclaw audit` can be called from a scheduled command job on the Mac mini and returns one agent's tool rows for the past week; to be tried once before the script is written.
That each row's tool name is specific enough for the counts to mean something for the tools Happy has by then (the page says tool actions show the tool name; no query was run).
Where saved notes live is settled by F041's own test (T6); that file change times in that folder reflect each save made through the sandbox was not tried.
safety: No model and no agent tool are involved. The script reads a record that holds tool names and outcomes but no content, and the file names in one parent's own notes folder. Its one text goes to that parent only, whose handle the jobs script reads from the family file; nothing goes into the other parent's chat.

name: Half page for Jordan: how to tell that Happy is down
description: Jordan gets one printed half page: how to recognise that Happy is down, that nothing in the house is broken, and who to call. After a power cut Happy stays down until Tony unlocks the Mac at home, as the roadmap row he chose says. There is no envelope, no password on paper and no Terminal step.
example: A power cut while Tony is out. Happy stops answering, and Jordan reads the half page: no reply within a few minutes means Happy is down, nothing is broken, and it comes back when Tony unlocks the Mac.
how: No software, so no house-rules rule. Tony writes and prints a half page for Jordan: (1) how to tell that Happy is down: no reply within a few minutes, or the error line a parent sees when a turn fails, worded from what test T8 showed on his own phone; (2) nothing is broken: after a power cut the Mac waits at the disk-unlock screen and Happy stays down until Tony unlocks it; (3) who to call. Not on the page and not built: an envelope, a password, Terminal commands, a pause phrase, an alert to her phone and the Legacy Contact step. The house scripts stay Tony-only.
depends_on: T8 run first (it belongs with the printed stop-and-check sheet, G005): Tony has seen on his own phone what a failed turn looks like, so the page is worded from that
Tony provides the 'who to call' line at execution
caveats: With the half page alone Jordan cannot bring Happy back: after a power cut Happy stays down until Tony unlocks the Mac at home, which is what the roadmap row he chose says.
A small UPS only bridges short cuts. A long outage still ends at the disk-unlock screen.
If Apple locks the Apple Account that Happy uses, nobody at home can fix it quickly, and iMessage is the only channel.
The page has no pause step: Jordan has no stop phrase of her own and is not a command owner.
Jordan gets no 'Happy is down' alert. She learns of an outage when she texts Happy and gets no answer.

An envelope so that she could restart Happy is not part of this card. If Tony ever wants one, his own unlock test (T10) comes first and it holds at most the happy user's password; an administrator credential on paper for anyone but Tony is a separate decision that has not been taken.
safety: Nothing is granted to any agent, and the page holds no credential and no command. No secret is typed into chat or stored in Happy's memory. The control plane stays Tony's alone.
unverified: What a parent sees on iMessage when a turn fails: read from the docs and the code, not tried (T8).

name: Paired-device deny list, deployed before the first device is paired
description: Just before the first device is paired (Tony's iPhone in OCL-01 or the virtual Mac of the screen-control pilot, MAC-02, whichever comes first), a short list in the Gateway config says which commands no paired phone or Mac may run: reading a phone's location, contacts, calendar, reminders, photos and motion, and driving, viewing or running commands on a Mac. The family sees no change; the pilot later lifts two entries for its own runs.
example: On the day his phone is paired Tony deploys the list, checks that the mail connector still works, and only then makes the setup code.
how: Config only, with no house-rules rule, written on the day the first device is paired, from the installed version's docs. `gateway.nodes.commands.deny` gets `computer.act`; the desktop host commands (`system.run`, `system.run.prepare`, `system.which`, `browser.proxy`, `browser.proxy.upload.v1`, `mcp.tools.call.v1`, `screen.snapshot`, `desktop.stream`); the iPhone data commands (`location.get`, `contacts.search`, `calendar.events`, `reminders.list`, `photos.latest`, `motion.activity`, `motion.pedometer`); and the four `talk.ptt.*` commands until Talk is set up. Nothing is added to `gateway.nodes.commands.allow`; `gateway.nodes.pluginTools.enabled: false`; pairing stays manual (`autoApproveLocal` and `sshVerify` false, `autoApproveCidrs` unset), and a Mac is never paired with a setup link. Deploy, confirm that the mail connector and any browser still work, and only then make a phone's setup code. After pairing, read the device's declared commands and deny any unwanted one by its exact name. happy-inspect's posture check gains the deny list, `sshVerify` and `pluginTools.enabled`. One rule, no code: never enable `cua-computer` on the Mac mini.
depends_on: No other card: an ordinary deploy, done on the day the first device is paired and before any setup code is made
caveats: Until that day nothing in config covers a device paired by mistake: with a setup code, a phone's default data reads would be live at once. The written rule meanwhile is no Mac app, no pairing and no setup code; the one documented line for screen control, `computer.act`, can ride along in any earlier deploy.

A setup code approves a device and its first command list in one step, so the list has to be deployed before the code is made, not after. For a Mac no setup link is used, so the device and then its command list are approved by hand in two steps.
The list is Gateway-wide, not per device: a pilot that lifts an entry lifts it for every paired device.

The list does not empty a device's commands. OpenClaw's defaults still allow `camera.list`, `device.info`, `device.status` and `system.notify` on an iPhone, so the phone's declared commands are read at pairing and any unwanted one is added.
If the check shows that the mail connector or a browser broke, `browser.proxy` and `mcp.tools.call.v1` come off the list while no Mac is paired and go back before any Mac is.
The `cua-computer` rule is a second lock: on macOS that route also needs the OpenClaw Mac app, which is not installed on the Mac mini, so no check code is written for it.
safety: Pure tightening: a limit in config that a prompt cannot change. Until the screen-control pilot no agent holds the `computer` tool, and none holds the nodes tools (each parent's agent denies `group:nodes` and the inbox agent has no tools), so a paired device gives agents nothing new.
unverified: That deny entries for `system.run` and the other host commands apply exactly as for `computer.act`; the docs state the rule for exact command names in general.
That denying `browser.proxy` and `mcp.tools.call.v1` for paired devices leaves the connectors and any browser on the Gateway itself untouched; checked on the day, when the mail connector exists.

Which command name sits behind the iPhone app's 'Screen snapshot' capability: the docs list `screen.snapshot` as a desktop command and do not name the phone's, so it is read from the phone at pairing and denied by its exact name.

name: Screen-control pilot on a clean, throwaway virtual Mac (attended by Tony)
description: An experimental pilot: Happy controls the screen of a clean, throwaway virtual Mac that holds no Apple Account, Messages or saved passwords, never Happy's own desktop. It starts with one 'step zero' test and ends there if that fails. If it passes, Tony starts and watches every run of one chore he names at execution; nobody starts a run by text.
example: Step zero: in the throwaway virtual Mac, one screenshot is taken and one click is made on an empty desktop while Tony watches. Later Tony starts the chore he named, watches it and reads the result: 'done' or 'stopped: a sign-in window appeared'.
how: Step zero first; if it fails the pilot ends, and no real desktop is ever used. A throwaway macOS guest on the Mac mini (for example with the Lume CLI); OpenClaw.app installed in it and paired by hand as its own device, with no setup link; proof that the app runs there without operator rights; then, with the MAC-04 entries for `computer.act` and `screen.snapshot` lifted, one screenshot and one click invoked by Tony as operator. If it passes: one `desk` agent with memory off, its own capped model key, the minimal tool profile and only `computer` (in its tool allow and in `tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow`); the guest may reach only the gateway and is reset before every run. Tony starts and watches each run, and stops it with 'Allow Computer Control' in the guest's app or by putting the deny entries back. Test: his chore, run a few times, once with a planted instruction on screen. House-rules plugin: no rule while only Tony starts runs.
depends_on: MAC-04 deny list in place first; its entries for `computer.act` and `screen.snapshot` are lifted for the pilot. The list is Gateway-wide, so no other Mac is paired meanwhile, and if a phone is paired by then its approved command list is re-read first
Tony provides the chore at execution: one family chore that no app or script already handles, with nothing from the never list in it (no payment, purchase, booking, lock or CAPTCHA)
Step zero passes; if it does not, the pilot ends there
Disk and memory on the Mac mini for a macOS guest (OpenClaw's virtual-Mac page asks for about 60 GB of free disk)

A route from the guest to the gateway, which listens on the Mac mini only: the guest's own tailnet identity or an SSH tunnel, limited to the gateway's address and reviewed as a change to the M0 baseline
Tony provides a new capped model key for the desk agent at execution, created by hand (each agent has its own key)
caveats: The guest is not empty of secrets: the app inside it is signed in to the family gateway. Until step zero shows it running as a device with no operator rights, the agent driving the screen could open a console to everything the clean desk was built to keep away.
Pairing the Mac app pairs a whole device: shell commands, a browser proxy, connector calls and a desktop stream arrive with pointer control. Those stay on the deny list.
There is no check per click and no approval per action: dozens of clicks run unreviewed, so Tony watches every run, and nothing sent by text stops a run in mid-task.

Red-team research on computer-use agents reports injected on-screen instructions succeeding in a large share of attempts, so the tool's built-in warning to the model is a tripwire, not a control. What exists on the controlled desktop is the real boundary.
A desktop that is never reset is the agent's memory: files, open windows and the clipboard carry over from one run to the next.
A pass shows that the chore can be done, not that screen control is safe. Letting anyone start a run by text would need a stop check in code first, as a rule in the house-rules plugin.
safety: The desk agent reads untrusted content (the screen) and holds no memory, accounts or message tool. Its limits are config a prompt cannot change: `computer` on that agent alone, every other device command on the deny list, a guest that reaches only the gateway and is reset before each run, with the app's operator access proven absent first. Never Happy's own desktop; nothing from the never list.
unverified: That OpenClaw.app's Computer Control (its macOS permissions, its capture path and its 'verified unlocked desktop' check) works inside a macOS guest with a virtual display. Step zero settles it.
Whether the Mac app can run in the guest as a device with no operator rights. Step zero settles it.
How to restrict a Lume guest's network to one host address.

That with `cua-computer` never enabled on the Mac mini, a `computer` call with no target lands on the guest and never on Happy's own desktop; the docs say the sole connected computer is used, and it was not run.

How Tony invokes one screenshot and one click as operator in step zero, and later starts a run on the desk agent and reads its result; the docs say an operator with write access can invoke a paired device's command, and none of this was tried.
Apple's licence for the installed macOS 27 (the macOS 26 licence, read in an earlier run, allows up to two additional macOS instances in virtual machines for personal use).
The guest's memory cost; OpenClaw's page states disk only.
